mechanism:
The hypothesis a > b > 0 is part of the one line, not a footnote to it, and it is what turns an identity into a loop.

Why the identity holds. Let d divide both a and b, say a = m*d and b = n*d. Then a - b = (m - n)*d, so d divides a - b, and d therefore divides both entries of the pair (a - b, b). Backwards: if d divides b and divides a - b, then it divides the sum (a - b) + b = a, so d divides both entries of (a, b). The two pairs have the identical SET of common divisors, not merely the same largest one, so their greatest common divisors are equal.

Why it is a loop. The identity may only be applied to a pair written with the larger entry first, because that is what a > b > 0 demands. So the rule itself, and nothing added to it, selects which of the two numbers is reduced: the larger one. Applying it sends the unordered pair {a, b} to {a - b, b}. Since a > b, a - b >= 1, so both entries are still positive whole numbers and the hypothesis can be met again as long as they differ.

Why it stops. Each application decreases the sum of the pair by b, and b >= 1, so the sum is a strictly decreasing sequence of integers bounded below by 2. It cannot decrease forever, so after finitely many steps the hypothesis can no longer be met with distinct entries, which happens exactly when the two numbers are equal. At that point the pair is {g, g}, and g divides itself, so g is the greatest common divisor of the original pair.

Outside a > b > 0 nothing here is claimed. At b = 0 the pair never changes; with a negative entry the pair can grow without bound, or halt on a negative value that is not the gcd; with a < b the rule simply does not apply until the pair is rewritten larger-first. The ordering is Euclid's own: Elements VII.1 sets out two UNEQUAL numbers and continually subtracts the less from the greater (f18). The positivity is not a quotation from him but a modern reading of him: David Joyce's commentary on the Book VII definitions says the numbers of Books VII-IX are whole positive numbers, and narrows that to whole positive numbers greater than 1, because Euclid treats the unit, 1, separately from numbers, 2, 3, and so forth (f19, f20). So a > b > 0 is very slightly wider than Euclid's own domain, which on that reading starts at 2. Nothing mathematical turns on the gap - the loop is correct at b = 1 - and the unit does appear inside his procedure rather than among its inputs: VII.1 runs until a unit is left (f21).

On 1920 and 1080 the loop runs {1920,1080} -> {1080,840} -> {840,240} -> {600,240} -> {360,240} -> {240,120} -> {120,120}: six subtractions to 120, and 1920/120 = 16 while 1080/120 = 9, which is the 16:9 of the 1080p mode.
title: Euclid's one-line loop.
